2022 IEEE Bombay Section Signature Conference (IBSSC)
Prediction of Anxiety Disorders using Machine Learning Techniques — Anika Kapoor, Shivani Goel

The paper focuses on using Machine Learning techniques to predict/classify different anxiety disorders such as Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), Panic Disorder (PD),  Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) and Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD). It investigates the use of ML algorithms for identifying anxiety disorders from questionnaire/survey-based data.
Machine Learning classification techniques including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Linear Regression and other ML algorithms are used to predict different anxiety disorders.

he study reviews the application of Machine Learning techniques for prediction of different anxiety disorders and compares the performance of different algorithms. SVM is reported as having the highest accuracy for GAD and SAD; for PTSD and OCD, other algorithms were reported to be slightly better, while Random Forest performed best for Panic Disorder.
Machine-learning based classification/prediction scheme. Data are collected through surveys/questionnaires → preprocessing → ML algorithms are applied → anxiety disorder is predicted/classified.

Rapid Anxiety and Depression Diagnosis in Young Children Enabled by Wearable Sensors and Machine Learning — Ryan S. McGinnis, Ellen W. McGinnis, Jessica Hruschak, Nestor L. Lopez-Duran, Kate Fitzgerald, Katherine L. Rosenblum, Maria Muzik
The paper proposes a rapid wearable-sensor method for identifying anxiety and depression in young children using a brief fear-induction task.
Children with and without an internalizing diagnosis; motion data from a 90-second wearable-sensor task
Not specified in the IEEE record
Motion features from the most clinically feasible 20-second task phase are evaluated with several models, including logistic regression.
The best logistic-regression model reports 80% diagnostic accuracy, showing the potential for faster screening of internalizing disorders.
The sample is pediatric and relatively small. The method is a screening aid and does not replace a clinical diagnosis.
Fear-induction task → wearable motion capture → temporal feature extraction → ML screening model → anxiety/depression risk estimate.

A Machine-Learning Model for Detecting Depression, Anxiety, and Stress from Speech — Mashrura Tasnim, Ramon E. Diaz-Ramos, Eleni Stroulia, Luis A. Trejo
The paper develops a speech-based machine-learning pipeline for estimating the severity of anxiety, depression and stress over repeated observations.
Longitudinal speech samples labeled with DASS-21 depression, anxiety and stress scores
Not specified in the IEEE record
Acoustic features are extracted from speech and VGG-19 representations are used with a one-dimensional convolutional neural network.
The longitudinal design accounts for co-occurring conditions and changing symptom severity. The model predicts the severity of anxiety, depression and stress from speech.
DASS-21 labels are self-reported, and speech patterns can vary by speaker, language and recording conditions. The paper does not establish clinical diagnosis from speech alone.
Speech recording → acoustic-feature extraction → VGG-19 representation → 1-D CNN → symptom-severity prediction.

Effect of Artifact Removal in Machine Learning Based Anxiety Screening Using EEG Signal — Nazmus Sakib, Md. Kafiul Islam, Tasnuva Faruk
The paper studies whether removing EEG artifacts improves machine-learning-based anxiety screening.
EEG data from 40 participants; 24 with anxiety and 16 without anxiety
Not specified in the IEEE record
A new artifact-removal procedure is applied, Hjorth parameters are extracted and an SVM classifier is used for screening.
Artifact removal improves classification accuracy by 14.67% for left-frontal channels and 8.31% for right-frontal channels.
The sample is limited to participants aged 18–25. Results depend on EEG quality, channel selection and the screening labels used.
EEG acquisition → artifact removal → Hjorth-parameter extraction → SVM classification → anxiety screening.

An Attention Guided Lightweight Network-Based Scheme for Anxiety Detection Using Multimodal Analysis of Single-Channel Wearable ECG and RSP Sensor Signals — Utsab Saha, Swojan Datta Sammya, Puja Saha, Shaikh Anowarul Fattah, Chandan Shahnaz
The paper presents a lightweight wearable-sensor model for detecting normal, light, moderate and severe anxiety states.
Single-channel wearable ECG and respiration (RSP) signals; FBDAWT-based ECG features
Not specified in the IEEE record
An attention-guided deep-learning network with a multi-objective loss uses multimodal ECG and RSP information for anxiety-stage classification.
The study targets four anxiety states and emphasizes a lightweight architecture suitable for wearable deployment.
The model needs validation across larger and more diverse populations and real-world settings. Anxiety labels and sensor placement may affect generalization.
Wearable ECG/RSP → time-frequency feature extraction → attention-guided lightweight network → anxiety-stage classification.

Predicting Anxiety Treatment Outcomes with Machine Learning — Marija Stanojevic, Lesley A. Norris, Philip C. Kendall, Zoran Obradovic
The paper applies machine learning to predict outcomes of anxiety treatment from baseline patient information.
Clinical treatment data from anxiety-focused therapy studies
Not specified in the IEEE record
Multiple machine-learning models are trained to predict treatment outcomes using pre-treatment clinical and demographic variables.
The work investigates whether baseline information can support individualized prediction of anxiety-treatment outcomes.
Treatment datasets may be limited in size and differ across studies. Predictions should support, not replace, clinician judgment.
Baseline clinical data → feature preparation → ML outcome prediction → treatment-response estimate.

Evaluation of Stress Response Using Smartphone PPG for Anxiety and Depression Monitoring — Diego Cajal, Concepción de la Cámara, Mar Posadas-de-Miguel, Noel Torrijos, Óscar Nadal, Teresa Blanco, Sara Sidd, Pablo Armañac, Eduardo Gil, Jesús Lázaro, Raquel Bailón
The paper evaluates smartphone-camera photoplethysmography as an accessible measure for monitoring anxiety and depression-related stress responses.
79 participants in the final analysis; 22 patients with generalized anxiety disorder and/or major depressive disorder and 57 controls
Not specified in the IEEE record
Pulse-rate-variability metrics from smartphone-camera PPG are compared with a validated reference device using correlation and Bland–Altman analyses.
Smartphone PPG shows high agreement with the reference device and identifies differences in stress reactivity between patient and control groups.
The protocol is controlled and the smartphone signal is sensitive to finger movement and tremor. Longitudinal and naturalistic validation is still needed.
Smartphone-camera PPG → pulse-rate-variability extraction → reference comparison → anxiety/depression stress-reactivity assessment.

Wearable Sensors and Machine Learning: Insights into Depression, Anxiety, and Emotional States and Changes — Wei Zhao, Kentaro Go
The paper reviews wearable-sensor and machine-learning approaches for monitoring anxiety, depression and emotional changes.
Studies published between 2013 and 2023; no original dataset
Not applicable (review paper)
The review compares wearable modalities, behavioral features and common models such as SVM and Random Forest for mental-health monitoring.
It identifies the prediction of emotional changes as an underexplored area and summarizes opportunities for wearable-based anxiety monitoring.
The review depends on heterogeneous prior studies and does not validate one common dataset or one clinical anxiety model.
Literature search → study selection → comparison of sensors, features and ML methods → research-gap analysis.

Comparative Assessment of Machine Learning Models for Detection of Mental Health of Students: A Case Study of Undergraduate Students — Sujal Zade, Nayan Potdukhe, Prateek Verma, Jampana Ruthvika
The paper screens undergraduate students for anxiety and depression-related mental-health risk using questionnaire responses and machine learning.
20-item Likert-scale questionnaire from 142 undergraduate students
Not specified in the IEEE record
Questionnaire data are normalized and evaluated with Logistic Regression, SVM, Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, Random Forest and KNN.
Logistic Regression and SVM report the strongest results, with 96.6% accuracy and an F1-score of 0.964 in the study.
The dataset comes from one rural engineering institution and uses self-reported responses. Screening performance may not generalize to other student populations.
Questionnaire → normalization → train/test split → classifier comparison → student anxiety/depression risk screening.

2017 IEEE International Conference on Smart Computing (SMARTCOMP)
FishBuddy: Promoting Student Engagement in Self-Paced Learning through Wearable Sensing — Jingjing Chen, Bin Zhu, Olle Bälter, Jianliang Xu, Weiwen Zou, Anders Hedman, Rongchao Chen, Mengdie Sang
The paper uses wearable sensing to detect frustration during self-paced learning and evaluate an intervention intended to reduce student anxiety.
20 first-year undergraduate students performing online English-grammar exercises; Apple Watch heart-rate data and self-reports
Not specified in the IEEE record
A physiologically aware performance-evaluation model identifies intervention moments and an Apple Watch application presents physiological feedback.
Students using FishBuddy reported lower anxiety and isolation and remained engaged longer, although exercise scores did not differ significantly.
The sample is small and limited to one learning activity. Anxiety reduction is based mainly on self-reported outcomes.
Learning activity → Apple Watch heart-rate monitoring → frustration detection → physiological feedback → anxiety and engagement evaluation.

2025 Third International Conference on Augmented Intelligence and Sustainable Systems (ICAISS)
IoT-based Mental Health Monitoring with Machine Learning — Neha Prabhakar Rajas, Anvi Kekane, Apoorv Patil, Apoorva Kulkarni, Arnav Bang, Arpit Verma
The paper proposes an IoT-based system for real-time monitoring of stress and anxiety using wearable physiological sensing.
Heart-rate data collected through an ESP32-based wearable-sensor system
Not specified in the IEEE record
Wearable signals are transmitted to a phone or cloud platform and analyzed using SVM and neural-network models for mental-health prediction.
The system is designed to provide real-time alerts and personalized recommendations for mental-health management, including anxiety-related monitoring.
The abstract does not provide a detailed clinical validation protocol or a public dataset. Real-world accuracy and privacy need further evaluation.
Wearable heart-rate sensing → ESP32 and cloud/mobile pipeline → SVM/neural network → anxiety/stress monitoring → alert.
